meta.title: Who really said "Teach Them to Yearn for the Vast and Endless Sea"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The idea is Saint-Exupery's, from Citadelle (1948). The famous English sentence is not: it is an anonymous paraphrase first documented in 1999.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Teach Them to Yearn for the Vast and Endless Sea'?
meta.ogDescription: Right author, wrong words. Quote Investigator finds no close match in Saint-Exupery's writings; the English wording surfaces in 1999.

answer.label: Not Saint-Exupéry’s words — a modern paraphrase of his
answer.authorDates: 1900–1944 · French writer, poet, journalist and aviator
answer.sourceLine: The thought really is Saint-Exupéry’s. It comes from section LXXV of Citadelle, the book published in 1948, four years after his death, and known in English as The Wisdom of the Sands. The famous English sentence is not his. Quote Investigator ↗ states flatly that “researchers have not found a close match for this statement in the works of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry,” and dates its earliest known appearance to a Usenet post in November 1999 — more than half a century after Citadelle appeared.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — the right author, but not his sentence.

source.excerpt: Celui-là tissera des toiles, l’autre dans la forêt par l’éclair de sa hache couchera l’arbre. L’autre, encore, forgera des clous, et il en sera quelque part qui observeront les étoiles afin d’apprendre à gouverner. Et tous cependant ne seront qu’un. Créer le navire ce n’est point tisser les toiles, forger les clous, lire les astres, mais bien donner le goût de la mer qui est un, et à la lumière duquel il n’est plus rien qui soit contradictoire mais communauté dans l’amour.
trail: Quote Investigator’s investigation ↗ is unambiguous on the wording: “Researchers have not found a close match for this statement in the works of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry.” Its conclusion is a hypothesis, not an attribution: “QI hypothesizes that the modern saying was derived from the passage written by Antoine de Saint-Exupéry in the ‘Citadelle’. Perhaps someone constructed a paraphrase that was later reassigned directly to Saint-Exupéry.”

The same page dates the English saying: “The first known instances of the English expression appeared relatively recently in the 1990s” — the earliest it documents being a November 1999 message on the Usenet newsgroup alt.callahans, followed by newspaper appearances in 2000 and 2004 and a teachers’ compilation in 2010, each with different wording.

We read Wikiquote’s Saint-Exupéry page ↗ in full. All three circulating English versions — including this one, word for word — sit in its Disputed section, under the note: “These appear to be loose paraphrases of this passage from Saint-Exupéry’s Citadelle (1948).” None appears in its sourced Citadelle section.

Wikipedia ↗ independently confirms the book’s status — it lists Citadelle (1948), English title The Wisdom of the Sands, among the works published posthumously — and gives his dates as 29 June 1900 to about 31 July 1944.
source.cutTag: Citadelle, section LXXV (1948) — the French original
source.excerptNote: In English, as Quote Investigator renders it ↗: “One will weave the canvas; another will fell a tree by the light of his ax. Yet another will forge nails, and there will be others who observe the stars to learn how to navigate. And yet all will be as one. Building a boat isn’t about weaving canvas, forging nails, or reading the sky. It’s about giving a shared taste for the sea, by the light of which you will see nothing contradictory but rather a community of love.” QI introduces it as “one possible rendering of this text into English” and names no translator; Wikiquote reproduces the same rendering ↗, citing QI. We could not consult a published edition of Citadelle ourselves.

source.rightsNote: Citadelle was first published in 1948, four years after Saint-Exupéry’s death and well after 1931, the current cut-off for the United States public domain — so the French text and its English translations are still in copyright. The popular English sentence is a separate matter again: it is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identified author and no published edition behind it.

author.heading: About Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
author.metaLine: 1900–1944 · French writer, poet, journalist and aviator
author.bio: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry (1900–1944) was a French writer, poet, journalist and pilot, born in Lyon to an aristocratic family and trained as a commercial aviator in the early 1920s. He flew airmail routes across Europe, Africa and South America, wrote Night Flight and Wind, Sand and Stars out of that work, and produced The Little Prince in wartime exile in the United States. He disappeared on a reconnaissance flight around 31 July 1944; Citadelle, the unfinished book this quotation is drawn from, was published in 1948.

copyAttribution: "If you want to build a ship, don't drum up the men and women to gather wood, divide the work, and give orders. Instead, teach them to yearn for the vast and endless sea." — a modern paraphrase, not Saint-Exupéry's words. The idea comes from section LXXV of his posthumous Citadelle (1948); the English saying first surfaces in 1999.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong words
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here. Saint-Exupéry did write about building a ship, and about the longing for the sea. He simply never wrote this sentence.

items.why: The circulating English sentence has no source in his work. Quote Investigator ↗: “Researchers have not found a close match for this statement in the works of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry.” It surfaces first in November 1999, in a Usenet post — fifty-one years after Citadelle was published.

“Teach them to long for the endless immensity of the sea” and “do not divide the men into teams and send them to the forest to cut wood” circulate just as widely. Wikiquote lists all three side by side ↗ in its Disputed section — which is itself the tell: a real translation of a real sentence does not come in three incompatible forms.

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: the idea is genuinely Saint-Exupéry’s, from section LXXV of Citadelle (1948); the English sentence people quote is an anonymous paraphrase first documented in 1999, per Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: It is a fixture of management writing, and its supposed author never wrote it. The paraphrase is sharper than the original — it turns a mystical passage about the unity of a shipyard into a clean instruction about motivating a team — which is precisely why it spread through conference slides and leadership books while the real passage stayed unread.
Saint-Exupéry never saw Citadelle published. He disappeared over the Mediterranean on a reconnaissance flight in July 1944, and the book was assembled from his drafts and issued four years later.
context.pull: The paraphrase is better copy than the original. That is exactly how it escaped.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI: 'Researchers have not found a close match for this statement in the works of Antoine de Saint-Exupery.'

QI's conclusion: it 'hypothesizes that the modern saying was derived from the passage written by Antoine de Saint-Exupery in the Citadelle. Perhaps someone constructed a paraphrase that was later reassigned directly to Saint-Exupery. The first known instances of the English expression appeared relatively recently in the 1990s.'

QI gives the French passage from Citadelle section LXXV beginning 'Celui-la tissera des toiles...' and introduces its English version as 'one possible rendering of this text into English', naming no translator.
QI's earliest documented instance of the popular English saying is a November 1999 message on the Usenet newsgroup alt.callahans, with later instances in 2000, 2004 and 2010 in differing wordings.

Wikiquote places all three circulating English versions, including 'teach them to yearn for the vast and endless sea', in its Disputed section, describing them as 'loose paraphrases of this passage from Saint-Exupery's Citadelle (1948)'.
Wikipedia lists Citadelle (1948), English title The Wisdom of the Sands, among Saint-Exupery's posthumously published works, and gives his dates as 29 June 1900 to about 31 July 1944.

A published English edition, The Wisdom of the Sands (1950), credited to Antoine de Saint-Exupery, exists at the Internet Archive (identifier wisdomofsands0000anto_b8b7); its metadata names no translator.
